entities.name: John II, Duke of Lorraine
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John II of Anjou, known as Duke of Lorraine from 1453 until his death on December 25, 1470, was a pivotal figure in the complex dynastic struggles of 15th-century Europe. As the eldest son of the formidable René of Anjou, King of Naples and Duke of Anjou, and Isabella, Duchess of Lorraine, John inherited a precarious position at the intersection of French, Burgundian, and Holy Roman Imperial interests. His reign was defined by relentless military campaigns aimed at asserting his family's claims to the Kingdom of Naples, as well as defending the autonomy of Lorraine against the encroaching ambitions of powerful neighbors like Duke Charles the Bold of Burgundy and King Louis XI of France.

John's military career began early, participating in the Hundred Years' War. However, his primary focus shifted to the Neapolitan succession after 1453, when he was named titular Duke of Calabria and dispatched to Italy to reclaim the Kingdom of Naples for the House of Anjou. From 1459 to 1462, he led a major expedition, achieving initial successes such as the Battle of Sarno in 1460, before suffering a decisive defeat at the Battle of Troia in 1462 against Ferdinand I of Naples. Back in France, he played a significant role in the War of the Public Weal (1465), a coalition of French feudal lords against Louis XI, and even briefly campaigned in England during the Wars of the Roses on behalf of the Lancastrian cause, notably at the Battle of Towton in 1461. He married Marie de Bourbon, daughter of Charles I, Duke of Bourbon, further entangling him in the French nobility's intricate web of alliances.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John II's persistent, though ultimately failed, attempts to secure the Kingdom of Naples had lasting regional consequences, solidifying Aragonese power in Southern Italy and contributing to the complex web of alliances and conflicts that led to the Italian Wars. His death also triggered a succession crisis in Lorraine that profoundly impacted the balance of power between France and Burgundy.
